svg.title: The device lifecycle as an attack surface: procurement, image, boot and configuration, with the check that closes each gap
svg.desc: A four-stage lifecycle across the top. Procurement: counterfeit or grey-market hardware with modified firmware, closed by buying through authorised channels, verifying serial numbers against the vendor, and recording the chain of custody. Image: a firmware file downloaded over TFTP from an unknown mirror, closed by verifying a signed hash before install, storing the reference hash out of band, and refusing unsigned images. Boot: an attacker with physical access interrupts the boot loader and changes the configuration register, closed by secure boot, a console password, physical locks and tamper-evident seals. Configuration: a baseline that reaches production unverified, closed by golden configuration with automated comparison, drift detection, and a rollback path. A side panel shows the three questions to ask a vendor in writing: can we verify the image signature, do you publish hashes and notices for vulnerabilities per release, and what is your end-of-support date for this model. A footer states that the supply chain is not a procurement problem but a lifecycle one - every stage hands something to the next, and an unverified image makes every later control optional.
svg.text: The supply chain is a lifecycle, and each stage hands something to the next
An unverified image makes every control that follows optional - the ACL protects nothing if the ACL engine is not the one you bought.
nobody checks this until an audit
a rack in a shared cage is access
that nobody compared to the design
"it was configured by hand" is the cause
THREE QUESTIONS TO PUT IN THE CONTRACT
Can we verify the image signature
ourselves, with a key we hold?
not "is it signed", but "can we check"
Do you publish hashes and a
if not, version tracking is guesswork
What is the end-of-support date for
the model you cannot patch is the model you must replace
The chain has one property worth remembering: each stage trusts the previous one. Break stage two and the remaining three verify nothing.

Practical minimum for most enterprises: images only from an internal mirror, hash checked at install, golden config compared weekly, and device serials reconciled against the purchase record once a year.
The uncomfortable part: if an attacker has physical access, boot integrity is the only control left, and most enterprise switches ship without it enabled.
Document the reference hashes somewhere other than the device, or the check is self-referential and worthless.
